meta.title: Unified Ontology of Hungarian Linguistics (GOLD&OntoLing-based)
meta.description: Hungarian-language instantiation of the Unified Ontology of General and Theoretical Linguistics. The original general ontology is retained as the structural backbone; Hungarian-specific phonological, morphological, syntactic, semantic, orthographic and interface values are added as language-specific instances and constraints.

meta.method: Retain the source ontology taxonomy and terminology; instantiate language-dependent categories for Hungarian rather than replacing the universal layer.

Language.definition: GOLD&OntoLing: A complex, lawfully developing sign system that is part of human consciousness. It is organized as a lexicon and a grammar, ensuring the transfer of information from a mental form to a physical one. The most fundamental means of human communication. Language is a purely human activity, although some animals have communication systems which have certain analogies to human language. All human beings use language to interact with other members of the same speech community. Language is not only used as an instrument of communication, however, but also as a means of individual expression. Language is not instinctive; it has to be learnt as a system of arbitrary conventional symbols. Such symbols are primarily vocal, produced by the so-called organs of speech, but secondary systems such as writing and other codes may complement the vocal system. Some linguists, such as F. de Saussure, have stressed the view of language as general patterns in the speech of a community and as the speaking activity of an individual in a particular situation; others, with N. Chomsky, regard language as the innate capability of native speakers to understand and form grammatical sentences and as the actual utterances produced at a given time. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Language]

components.Lexicon: The inventory of sign units (words and morphemes).
components.Grammar: The set of rules for operating on these units.

Language_vs_Speech.Language: The abstract system; exists in the minds of speakers.
Language_vs_Speech.Speech: The concrete realization of language in communication; proceeds in time.

Linguistic_System.definition: GOLD: A term used to describe a language as a whole, with each of its component parts functioning according to an overall convention of usage to enable the members of a speech community to interchange information. Most linguists agree on a 'system of systems', i.e. the arrangement of units on hierarchically ordered and inter-related levels. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticSystem]

Linguistic_Taxon.definition: GOLD: The class of Taxons whose instances are used in the scientific classification of language varieties. That is, instances of LinguisticTaxon have instances that are human language varieties. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticTaxon]

Taxon.definition: GOLD: The class of scientific categories used to create a taxonomy and determined according to scientific principles in a given domain, e.g., Biology or Linguistics. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Taxon]

Genetic_Taxon.definition: GOLD: The class of all taxons whose members are based on genetic relatedness. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GeneticTaxon]

Context_of_Use_Taxon.definition: GOLD: The class of taxons whose instances classify language varieties according to how they are primarily used. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/ContextOfUseTaxon]

Geographic_Taxon.definition: GOLD: The class of linguistic taxons whose instances are groupings based on where, in general, the language varieties are used, e.g., AustralianLanguage. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GeographicTaxon]

Political_Taxon.definition: GOLD: The class of taxons whose instances are groupings based on political entities such as states or countries or larger politically defined entities, e.g., CameroonianLanguage. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PoliticalTaxon]

Endangerment_Taxon.definition: GOLD: There are a number of ways to categorize language endangerment situations. One useful taxonomy takes into account the relative rate of attrition together with its causes. This taxonomy recognizes four different categories of attrition: sudden, radical, gradual and top to bottom. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/EndangermentTaxon]

Language_Family.definition: GOLD: Group of languages that are genetically related, i.e can be traced to a common proto-language. The ordering of languages into a common language family is usually based on phonological, morphological, and lexical correspondences that stem from the proto-language. ... it refers to the largest spectrum of languages for which a genetic relationship can be demonstrated. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LanguageFamily]

Language_Stock.definition: GOLD: A term used for postulated but undemonstrated higher-order, more inclusive families (proposed but as yet unproven distant genetic relationships). [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LanguageStock]

Language_Subfamily.definition: GOLD: LanguageSubfamily (also called subgroup or branch) refers 'to a group of languages within a language family which are more closely related to each other than to other languages of that family.' [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LanguageSubfamily]

Isolate.definition: GOLD: Isolate is the class of human language varieties such that there are no other varieties that are genetically related. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Isolate]

Dialect.definition: GOLD: A regional, temporal or social variety of a language, differing in pronunciation, grammar and vocabulary from the standard language, which is in itself a socially favoured dialect. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Dialect]

The_Linguistic_Sign.definition: GOLD&OntoLing: A fundamental unit establishing a conventional relation between form and content. An abstract structure whose instances participate in a linguistic system, or language. By definition, a linguistic sign must have a form component (whose elements are phonological units), a grammatical component (whose elements are grammatical units), and a meaning component (whose elements are semantic units). The formal structure of a linguistic sign is determined by the grammar of a language. The information value of a linguistic sign, its meaning, is not fixed, but determined by the conventions of the language. The relation of form to meaning is largely arbitrary within a semiotic system. Signs are classified primarily according to what kinds of formal relations they participate in, and, secondly, according to their complexity (whether they are atomic or composed of other signs). Signs range from morphological and syntactic constructions to whole discourse segments. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticSign]

components.Signifier: The external form (sound or written representation).

properties.Arbitrariness: No natural relation between signifier and signified.
properties.Linear_Character: Elements follow one another in time.
properties.Double_Articulation: Signs are composed of smaller meaningful signs (primary) and non-meaningful units (secondary).

The_Linguistic_Sign.examples: Words and morphemes are the primary linguistic signs.

Linguistic_Unit.definition: GOLD: This term is often used in linguistics and phonetics to refer to any entity which constitutes the focus of an enquiry. The unit is the stretch of language that carries grammatical patterns, and within which grammatical choices are made. For example, the unit sentence consists of one or more instances of the unit clause, and so on. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticUnit]

Form_Unit.definition: GOLD: Denotes the sensorily perceptible aspect of the linguistic sign. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FormUnit]

Grammar_Unit.definition: GOLD: A GrammarUnit is the structural component of the linguistic sign and includes notions such as morpheme, syntactic word, and construction. Grammar units are classified according to their mereology (part-whole and complexity), morphosyntactic function, and whether they exist in a bound or free forms. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GrammarUnit]

Semantic_Unit.definition: GOLD: A SemanticUnit is the class of semantics elements, or units of semantic structure (sometimes called a sememe). Semantic units serve as the meaning component of linguistic signs. A semantic unit is intended for linguistic description and no particular logical representation is implied. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SemanticUnit]

Linguistic_Expression.definition: GOLD: A LinguisticExpression is any physical form (sound, visual image or sequence thereof) used to represent a linguistic unit. A linguistic expression may be spoken, written, or signed. A linguistic expression is distinct form the actual process (speaking, writing, signing) that produces the expression. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticExpression]

Spoken_Linguistic_Expression.definition: GOLD: A SpokenLinguisticExpression is the physical sound form of language as distinct from either signed or spoken expressions. A spoken expression is the sound that is produced (and perceived) during a speaking event. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SpokenLinguisticExpression]

Written_Linguistic_Expression.definition: GOLD: A WrittenLinguisticExpression is the written physical form of language as distinct from either signed or spoken expressions. A written expression is the physical product of the writing process. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/WrittenLinguisticExpression]

Signed_Linguistic_Expression.definition: GOLD: A SignedLinguisticExpression is the signed physical form of language as distinct from either written or spoken expressions. Signed expressions are the primary means in which sign languages are transmitted. A signed expression is the image sequence that is produced (and perceived) during a signing event. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SignedLinguisticExpression]

Linguistic_Property.definition: GOLD: LinguisticProperty is the class of properties that pertain to linguistic units. A unit's properties determine its behavior in a grammatical system. Specific kinds of properties are relevant to certain types of units. In some language, for example, tense properties may be relevant for verbs. See also Feature and FeatureValue for the corresponding data structure for properties. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticProperty]

Linguistic_Data_Structure.definition: GOLD: A linguistic data structure is an abstract container for grouping together instances of linguistic data, usually to suit a particular theory or computational implementation. Examples include: feature structures, lexical entries, and paradigms. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LinguisticDataStructure]

Literary_Language.definition: OntoLing: The codified, supra-dialectal, polyfunctional standard form.

Non-literary_Varieties.Territorial_Dialects: Systems functioning in a part of the language's territory.
Non-literary_Varieties.Social_Dialects: Systems used among certain social groups.
Non-literary_Varieties.Vernacular: Language of non-educated people with deviations from the norm.

Human_Language_Variety.definition: GOLD: A term used in sociolinguistics and stylistics to refer to any system of linguistic expression whose use is governed by situational variables. In some cases, the situational distinctiveness of the language may be easily stated, as in many regional and occupational varieties; in other cases, as in studies of social class, the varieties are more difficult to define, involving the intersection of several variables. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/HumanLanguageVariety]

Attested_Variety.definition: GOLD: A linguistic form for which there is evidence of present or past use. Attestation refers to something that is found in actual recorded usage, compared with the hypothetical predictions of grammar or the intuitive (but otherwise unsupported) observations of the linguist. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/AttestedVariety]

Described_Variety.definition: GOLD: The class of distinct human languages or language varieties as recognized by a linguist or a particular linguistic community, but not necessarily recognized by the ISO 639-3 standard. This category allows a language to be described even though it is not (yet) included in ISO 639-3. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/DescribedVariety]

Extinct_Variety.definition: GOLD: A language no longer used as a medium of oral communication in a speech community, e.g. Latin, Gothic, as opposed to living languages such as English, Japanese. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/ExtinctVariety]

Living_Variety.definition: GOLD: A language which is the current native language of a speech community. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LivingVariety]

Nearly_Extinct_Variety.definition: GOLD: The class of languages that have relatively few native speakers. A nearly extinct variety is expected to become extinct in a short time period, e.g., Jebero or Wichita. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/NearlyExtinctVariety]

Second_Language_Only_Variety.definition: GOLD: A language variant that has no mother tongue speakers. It is only spoken as a second language. One example would be the case of Callawalla (caw), which is only learned in adolescence. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SecondLanguageOnlyVariety]

Signed_Language.definition: GOLD: SignLanguage or SignSystem is referring to the system of manual communication used by certain groups as an alternative to oral communication. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SignedLanguage]

Spoken_Language.definition: GOLD: One of the modes of linguistic communication. As distinct from written language, it is characterized by repetition, hesitation forms, pauses, variations in articulation, lapses, as well as differences in vocabulary and grammar. The primary importance spoken language in the analysis, description and teaching of languages has been stressed frequently. Alternative terms: speech, conversation. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SpokenLanguage]

Written_Language.definition: GOLD: One of the means or modes of linguistic communication. As distinct from spoken language, it does not usually represent all features of speech such as stress and pitch, and lacks the redundancy and lapses of spoken conversation (written dialogue and reading aloud are more akin to written than to spoken language). Also reference orthography. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/WrittenLanguage]

Unattested_Variety.definition: GOLD: UnattestedVariety is the class of language varieties that are posited to exist or to have existed. Examples include reconstructed languages, such as Proto-Indo-European. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/UnattestedVariety]

Thing.definition: GOLD: In Web Ontology Language, Thing is the superclass of all classes. The most basic concepts in a domain should correspond to classes that are the roots of various taxonomic trees. Every individual in the OWL world is a member of the class owl:Thing. Thus each user-defined class is implicitly a subclass of owl:Thing. Domain specific root classes are defined by simply declaring a named class. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Thing]

Abstract.definition: GOLD: Properties or qualities as distinguished from any particular embodiment of the properties/ qualities in a physical medium. Instances of Abstract can be said to exist in the same sense as mathematical objects such as sets and relations, but they cannot exist at a particular place and time without some physical encoding or embodiment. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Abstract]

Object.definition: GOLD: Corresponds roughly to the class of ordinary objects. Examples include normal physical objects, geographical regions, and locations of processes, the complement of objects in the physical class. In a 4D ontology, an object is something whose spatiotemporal extent is thought of as dividing into spatial parts roughly parallel to the time-axis. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Object]

Process.definition: GOLD: The class of things that happen and have temporal parts or stages. Examples include extended events like a football match or a race, actions like pursuing and reading, and biological processes. The formal definition is: anything that occurs in time but is not an object. Note that a process may have participants 'inside' it which are objects, such as the players in a football match. In a 4D ontology, a process is something whose spatiotemporal extent is thought of as dividing into temporal stages roughly perpendicular to the time-axis. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Process]

Feature_System.definition: GOLD: An utterance is divided into parts, which are assigned to word classes and then subclassified in terms of their 'accidents' or properties. The properties, also referred to as features or categories, express what is shared by different linguistic elements, as opposed to what is idiosyncratic. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureSystem]

Feature_Structure.definition: GOLD: A FeatureStructure is a set of one or more FeatureSpecifications. A FeatureStructure is a kind of information structure, a container or data structure, used to group together qualities or features of some object. In a grammatical feature system, a FeatureStructure holds the grammatical information associated with some linguistic unit. In a typed feature system, a FeatureStructure has an associated type, usually a PartOfSpeech. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureStructure]

Feature_Specification.definition: GOLD: A FeatureSpecification is a data structure that groups together a linguistic feature with a value. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureSpecification]

Simple_Specification.definition: GOLD: A SimpleSpecification is a kind of FeatureSpecification whose value must be a simple linguistic attribute. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SimpleSpecification]

Complex_Specification.definition: GOLD: A ComplexSpecification is a kind of FeatureSpecification whose value must be a FeatureStructure. This class gives a feature system its recursive properties. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/ComplexSpecification]

Feature_Constraint.definition: GOLD: A term used in linguistics, and especially in generative grammar, to refer to a condition which restricts the application of a rule, to ensure that the sentences generated are well formed. For example, in generative phonology, a distinction can be made between 'simultaneous' and 'sequential' constraints: the former states the restrictions on the simultaneous occurrence of features, e.g. a segment cannot be at once [+high] and [+low]; the latter states the restrictions on sequences of features, e.g. whether a language permits consonant clusters. In generative syntax there are also several constraints which have to be imposed in order to prevent the derivation of ill formed phrase-markers, e.g. constraints on the ordering of rules. The notion of constraints takes on a different direction in optimality theory, where it is the principle explanatory device. Here, constraints are ways of characterizing language universals. Each language has its own ranking of constraints (e.g. which determine morpheme position or syllable structure), and differences between these rankings result in the variations observed between languages. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureConstraint]

Feature_Assignment_System.definition: GOLD: (The term 'assignment') was first used with respect to feature values by Corbett (1991) in his discussion of mechanisms for allotting nouns to different genders. Native speakers have the ability to 'work out' the gender of a noun, and models of this ability have been called 'gender assignment systems'. So far, the concept of 'assignment of a feature value' has not been used outside gender. For some features, there may not be as much to say as for gender. However, using the concept of 'assignment' with respect to the values of all features is useful to be able to compare the features. Therefore, for this typology I have adopted the following definition: an assignment system is a set of rules that realise the value of a feature on an element. Note, however, that under this definition, a gender value is 'assigned' both to nouns, and to targets of agreement in gender with the noun. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureAssignmentSystem]

Semantic_Assignment_System.definition: GOLD: For natural language understanding, the process of fine-grain semantic role assignment is one of the prominent steps, which provides semantic relations between constituents. The sense and sense relations between constituents provide the core meaning of a sentence. Abstract semantic roles include thematic roles, such as agent, theme, and instrument, and secondary roles such as location, time, and manner. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SemanticAssignmentSystem]

Formal_Assignment_System.definition: GOLD: One more distinction can be made within both types of inherently assigned feature values: that between formal and semantic assignment. This distinction was proposed by Corbett (1991) to account for the criteria according to which nouns can be allotted to genders. Corbett demonstrates that gender assignment systems in languages can be semantic or semantic-and-formal – that is, the set of rules that determine the assignment of inherent gender values to nouns refer to the meaning of words, or a combination of the meaning of words and the form of words. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FormalAssignmentSystem]

Feature_Distribution_System.definition: GOLD: In a given language, the system according to which feature values (of a particular feature) are determined contextually for elements, through agreement or government. FeatureDistributionSystem can have one or two main components: FeatureAgreementSystem, and FeatureGovernmentSystem. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureDistributionSystem]

Feature_Agreement_System.definition: GOLD: A type of FeatureDistributionSystem; in a given language, it is the system according to which feature values (of a particular feature) are determined for elements through agreement (i.e. where the form of the element is determined by the presence of another element). [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureAgreementSystem]

Feature_Government_System.definition: GOLD: The feature of case is typically involved in government. A governor does not bear the feature value it requires of its governee. Government is also asymmetric with regard to the possession of the feature specification by the elements. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/FeatureGovernmentSystem]

Interlinear_Glossed_Text.definition: GOLD: Interlinear glossed text (IGT) is a linguistic data structure meant to display morphosyntactic structure: morphemes, morpheme boundaries, morpheme types (clitics, prefixes, reduplicated forms), morphosyntactic features/values and part of speech information. At a minimum, an instance of IGT includes a single line of source language followed by a translation line. Often, a second gloss line is included to show detailed morphosyntactic structure using both words and phrases from the target language and various labels, or 'grams', that indicate morphosyntactic features/values, etc. It is possible to include separate lines for the orthographic form, phonetic form, and phonological form. Standards for IGT include the Leipzig Glossing Rules. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/InterlinearGlossedText]

Term.definition: GOLD: A vocabulary item which has a special meaning in a particular subject field, e.g. 'sound' or 'voice' in phonetics, or 'butterfly' in swimming. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Term]

Termset.definition: GOLD: A set of scientific terms used as part of an annotation system, usually the standard terms from a particular linguistic theory. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Termset]

Structural_Description.definition: GOLD: A term used in (esp. classical) transformational grammar to refer to an analysis of a terminal string in terms of a labeled bracketing. In transformational analysis, the SD identifies the input to a transformational rule: it specifies which phrase-markers are to be affected by the rule. i.e. which will 'satisfy' or 'meet' the conditions of the rule. The terms structural analysis and structure index are also used. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/StructuralDescription]

Ontology.definition: GOLD: An explicit specification of a representational vocabulary for a shared domain of discourse. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Ontology]

Citation.definition: GOLD: The action of citing or quoting any words or written passage from a publication that allows others to locate and identify the original source. Typical details include the title, author's name, the journal title (for articles), publication date and page numbers used in research. Note: This concept was included in order to facilitate linking to the bibliographic entries referenced in GOLD. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Citation]

Annotation_Property.definition: GOLD: 'Linguistic annotation' covers any descriptive or analytic notations applied to raw language data. The basic data may be in the form of time functions - audio, video and/or physiological recordings - or it may be textual. The added notations may include transcriptions of all sorts (from phonetic features to discourse structures), part-of-speech and sense tagging, syntactic analysis, 'named entity' identification, co-reference annotation, and so on. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/AnnotationProperty]

Class.definition: GOLD: This term refers to a set of entities, be they words, morphemes or otherwise, which share certain formal or semantic properties. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Class]

Symmetric_Property.definition: GOLD: Properties may be stated to be symmetric. If a property is symmetric, then if the pair (x,y) is an instance of the symmetric property P, then the pair (y,x) is also an instance of P. For example, friend may be stated to be a symmetric property. Then a reasoner that is given that Frank is a friend of Deborah can deduce that Deborah is a friend of Frank. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SymmetricProperty]

Transitive_Property.definition: GOLD: Those grammatical features which are used systematically to express certain relationships between the participants in a communicative situation and the actions, states, or circumstances in which they are involved. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/TransitiveProperty]

Hungarian_Language_Instance.label: Hungarian / magyar
Hungarian_Language_Instance.definition: Language-specific instance of the abstract Language class in the source ontology.

family_classification.note: The family/branch labels are taxonomic metadata; they do not alter the universal linguistic classes in the ontology.

geographic_distribution: Central Europe / Carpathian Basin Hungarian-speaking communities

orthography.script: Latin alphabet with Hungarian-specific diacritics and digraphs/trigraphs
orthography.digraph_trigraph_status: cs, dz, dzs, gy, ly, ny, sz, ty, zs are alphabetic units in Hungarian orthographic ordering.

typological_profile.case_marking: Primarily suffixal case marking with vowel-harmonic allomorphy; analyses differ in how case vs. postposition-like forms are counted.
typological_profile.word_order: No single rigid basic order; SOV is a common neutral descriptive generalization, while information structure strongly conditions constituent order.
typological_profile.head_directionality: Mixed; nominal modification is predominantly prenominal, while many adpositions are postpositional.

information_structure.focus: Identificational/exhaustive focus is associated with a preverbal focus position and can affect the position of the verb.
information_structure.distributive_quantification: Preverbal operator positions occur in analyses of Hungarian clause structure.

Phonetics.definition: OntoLing: The branch of linguistics studying the sound side of speech communication.

Substantive_Phonetics.definition: OntoLing: Studies physical and physiological aspects.

sub-branches.Articulatory: Anatomy and physiology of speech production.
sub-branches.Acoustic: Physical properties of the sound signal.

Linguistic_Phonetics_Phonology.definition: OntoLing: Studies the function of sound means in language, focusing on phonemes.

types.Synchronic: System at a specific point in time.

Phonetic_Units.definition: OntoLing: Linear objects that can follow one another.

Suprasegmental_Prosodic_Units.definition: OntoLing: Units consisting of segmental units.

Phonetic_Features.Suprasegmental_Features: Features applying to groups of segments (e.g., stress, intonation).

Phonetic_Rules.definition: OntoLing: Rules governing the use and variation of phonetic units.

Sound_Speech_Sound.definition: OntoLing: A concrete sound unit produced in a specific situation; material, infinite, continuous.

Sound_Type_Sound_of_Language.definition: OntoLing: An abstract unit grouping phonetically similar sounds considered one unit by native speakers.
Sound_Type_Sound_of_Language.relation: More abstract than a sound, less abstract than a phoneme.

Phoneme.definition: GOLD&OntoLing: An abstract, invariant unit of language used to form and distinguish signifiers. A phoneme is the underlying sound in a set of phonetically distinct sounds that native speakers of a language judge to be identical. Variants of the underlying sound are the product of systematic rules that modify the segment depending on the phonological context in which it occurs. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Phoneme]
Phoneme.function: Primary function is to distinguish meaningful units.
Phoneme.realization: In speech, realized as a sound or sound type.

Segment.definition: GOLD: A discrete unit that can be identified in the stream of speech, either physically or auditorily. Features that extend over more than one segment, such as pitch or stress, are termed suprasegmentals. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Segment]

Suprasegmental.definition: GOLD: Phonetic features extending over more than one segment, such as stress, length, tone, and intonation, which are not properties of single consonants or vowels. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Suprasegmental]

Syllable.definition: GOLD&OntoLing: Unit larger than a segment, with a peak of sonority. Ladefoged contends that there is no satisfactory definition for this unit of speech, but that syllables seem to be necessary units in the mental organization and production of utterances. However, Crystal defines the syllable as an element of speech that acts as a unit of rhythm, consisting of a vowel, syllabic, or vowel/consonant combination. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Syllable]

Toneme.definition: GOLD: A stress or tonal element which in a tone language distinguishes two otherwise identical words or forms. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Toneme]

Mora.definition: GOLD: Mora refers to the several parts of the phoneme which may receive divergent tonal treatments. A mora also can refer to a minimal unit of metrical time equivalent to a short syllable. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Mora]

Foot.definition: GOLD: Used to describe the unit of rhythm in languages displaying isochrony, i.e. where the stressed syllables fall at approximately regular intervals throughout an utterance. It is an extension of the term used in traditional studies of metrical verse structure, where the many regular patterns of stressed/unstressed syllables were given a detailed classification. In a more general phonological sense, the notion is applied to any utterance in a stress-timed language, not just verse. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Foot]

Speech_Apparatus.definition: OntoLing: The set of human organs used for sound production.

Articulators.Active: Organs that move (e.g., lower lip, tongue).
Articulators.Passive: Targets for active articulators (e.g., upper lip, teeth, palate).

Speech_Apparatus.Speech_Tract: Space from vocal cords to lips where articulation occurs.

Articulation.definition: OntoLing: Coordinated movement/position of speech organs shaping the vocal tract.

key_parameters.Place_of_Articulation: Localization of constriction (active and passive articulator).

Initiation.definition: OntoLing: Creation of an air stream.

Phonation.definition: OntoLing: Modulation of the air stream in the larynx.
Phonation.key_mechanism: Vocal fold vibration (voiced) or lack thereof (voiceless).

Acoustic_Phonetics.definition: OntoLing: Study of physical properties of the speech signal.

source-filter_theory.source: Aeroacoustic energy from vocal folds or constriction.
source-filter_theory.filter: Frequency-selective properties of the vocal tract (formants).

Perceptual_Phonetics.definition: OntoLing: Study of how the auditory system analyzes and identifies speech sounds.

Vowels_vs_Consonants.Vowels: Produced without significant obstruction; no noise; form syllable peak.
Vowels_vs_Consonants.Consonants: Produced with obstruction; noise present; localized articulation.

Consonant.definition: GOLD: A type of sound segment defined by closure or constriction of the vocal tract, which produces an audible friction. The vocal tract constriction does not have to result in complete blocking; it can simply be a restriction of air flow. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Consonant]

by_sonority.Sonorants: Strong acoustic energy; no voicing assimilation.

by_additional_articulation.Palatalization: Tongue body towards hard palate ('soft' consonants).
by_additional_articulation.Velarization: Tongue body towards soft palate ('hard' consonants).

Vowel.definition: GOLD: One of the two general categories used for the classification of speech sounds, the other being consonant. Phonetically, they are sounds articulated without a complete closure in the mouth that would produce a stop or a degree of narrowing that would create audible friction; the air escapes evenly over the center of the tongue. For oral vowels, air escapes solely through the mouth. If some air is simultaneously released through the nose, the vowel is nasal. The quality of the vowel sound is affected by the shape of the oral resonance chamber, chiefly influenced by the position of the lips and the position of the tongue. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Vowel]

Traditional_Phonology.definition: OntoLing: Structuralist approach focused on phonemes and oppositions.

Moscow_Phonological_School.definition: OntoLing: Phoneme as a functional unit within morphemes.

Saint_Petersburg_Phonological_School.definition: OntoLing: Phoneme as a sound type with a distinctive function.

Prague_Phonological_School.definition: OntoLing: Structuralist school known for theory of oppositions.

Generative_Phonology.definition: OntoLing: Dynamic model using ordered rules.

Dynamic_Models.definition: OntoLing: Modern models focusing on constraints and interactions.

Phonological_System.definition: GOLD: The set of consonant and vowel units that make up the words of a language or language variety, a phonological system is a list of contrastive sounds used in a language that are capable of distinguishing between two words with different meanings together with the ranges of variety each sound has and where those variants are found. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PhonologicalSystem]

Orthographic_System.definition: GOLD: A system of the art and rules of spelling according to the accepted standards, i.e., the use of the written characters of a language for forming words and sentences in conformity with the rules conventionally recognized as correct. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/OrthographicSystem]

Syllable.definition: GOLD&OntoLing: Unit larger than a segment, with a peak of sonority. Ladefoged contends that there is no satisfactory definition for this unit of speech, but that syllables seem to be necessary units in the mental organization and production of utterances. However, Crystal defines the syllable as an element of speech that acts as a unit of rhythm, consisting of a vowel, syllabic, or vowel/consonant combination. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Syllable]

Stress.definition: OntoLing: Suprasegmental feature making a syllable more prominent.

Intonation.definition: OntoLing: Complex unit including pitch, intensity, and duration.

Phonetic_Word_and_Syntagma.Phonetic_Word: Group of words united by a single stress.
Phonetic_Word_and_Syntagma.Syntagma: Group of phonetic words united by intonation.

Phonological_Typology.definition: OntoLing: Study of the range and distribution of sound systems.

Applied_Phonetics.Graphics: Study of written signs and their correspondence to phonemes.

Phonetic_Property.definition: GOLD: The class of properties used to describe speech sounds. The properties given here are more or less taken directly from Ladefoged's later works, in particular, the taxonomies of Ladefoged. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PhoneticProperty]

Articulatory_Property.definition: GOLD: The class of properties defining how sounds are produced in the mouth. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/ArticulatoryProperty]

Acoustic_Property.definition: GOLD: The class of properties concerning the acoustic nature of speech sounds. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/AcousticProperty]

Laryngeal_Property.definition: GOLD: The laryngeal setting refers to differences in the timing of laryngeal activity in relation to oral articulation. Most languages have phonemic contrasts between classes of stops which differ in the mode of action of the larynx, or in the timing of laryngeal activity. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LaryngealProperty]

Supralaryngeal_Property.definition: GOLD: The supralaryngeal node dominates the activity of all of the articulators except stiffening and slacking of the vocal folds. For consonants it can be viewed as the default node which comes into play when the supranasal node below it is deactivated. In the case of sounds produced by an articulator dominated by this node, the only possible segments are those which are traditionally classified as [-consonantal]. It is not necessary to specify manner features for sounds dominated by the supralaryngeal node, because they are redundantly determined. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/SupraLaryngealProperty]

Nasality_Property.definition: GOLD: The class of properties that describe the degree to which the velum or soft palate is raised or lowered, allowing or prohibiting air from escaping through the nose. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/NasalityProperty]

Place_Property.definition: GOLD: The superclass of properties that specify the location of the articulators. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PlaceProperty]

Manner_Property.definition: GOLD: A sound property referring to the kind of articulatory process used in a sound's production. The distinction between vowel and consonant is usually made in terms of manner of articulation. Within consonants, several articulatory types are recognized based on the type of closure made by the vocal organs. Within vowels, classification is based on the number of auditory qualities distinguishable in the sound, the position of the soft palate, and the type of lip position. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/MannerProperty]

Stricture_Property.definition: GOLD: A general term used in Phonetics to refer to an articulation which restricts the airstream to some degree, ranging from a complete closure to a slight narrowing. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/StrictureProperty]

Voicing_Property.definition: GOLD: Refers to the vibratory activity of the vocal folds. Most languages have phonemic contrasts between voiced and voiceless sounds (regular vibration of the vocal folds versus no vibration of the vocal folds respectively). However, Ladefoged and Maddieson recognize five steps in the continuum of modes of vibration in the glottis, going from breathy voice - the most open setting of the vocal folds in which vibration will occur, passing through slack voice, modal voice, and stiff voice, ending with creaky voice - the most constricted setting in which vibration will occur. Each of these modes of voicing may or may not be phonemic in a given language. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/VoicingProperty]

Glottal_Stricture_Property.definition: GOLD: The three phonation types are part of the five possible values of Glottal Stricture that are used by languages. Sounds can have the vocal cords tightly together, as in a glottal stop, or they can be far apart as in voiceless sounds, or they can have one of the three phonation types: breathy voice, modal voice and creaky voice. Although some phoneticians have shown how terms similar to these may be combinable from the phonetic point of view, the named terms form a set of phonologically mutually exclusive possibilities. These factors point to there being an ordered set of five possibilities: [voiceless], [breathy], [modal voice], [creaky] and [closed]. It is certainly appropriate to consider these glottal states as resulting from two physiological attributes of the vocal cords, their stiffness and their aperture. However from a linguistic point of view, the named values of the feature Glottal Stricture operate as a linearly ordered set of five mutually exclusive possibilities. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GlottalStrictureProperty]

Glottal_Timing_Property.definition: GOLD: A phonation type containing the features 'aspirated' and 'unaspirated. Aspiration involves matters of relative timing between laryngeal and oral articulations, and the wider opening can be viewed as an aspect of the control of this timing. There are two ways of interpreting this greater width; it can be seen as the essential aspect of the production of voiceless aspiration, that is, aspiration is an extra-wide opening of the vocal folds [Kim 1965], or it can be seen as a by-product of the mechanism by which a delay between the offset of the oral and glottal gestures is achieved, that is, aspiration is essentially a matter of the timing between speech movements controlling laryngeal setting and oral articulation [Goldstein and Browman 1986]. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GlottalTimingProperty]

Glottal_Movement_Property.definition: GOLD: A phonation type containing the features 'raising' and 'lowering'. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/GlottalMovementProperty]

Airstream_Property.definition: GOLD: Refers to the direction of the airstream in speech sound production. In the canonical literature, there are three airstream mechanisms: pulmonic, velaric, and glottalic. Glottalic airstream mechanism is sometimes used to describe the method of production of ejectives and implosives. Ladefoged and Maddieson prefer to regard implosives and ejectives as characterized by a laryngeal parameter of movement rather than an airstream property. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/AirstreamProperty]

Pulmonic_Property.definition: GOLD: Pulmonic refers to an air-stream mechanism wherein the air is generated in the lungs and pushed out under the control of the respiratory muscles. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PulmonicProperty]

Velaric_Property.definition: GOLD: Velaric refers to an air-stream mechanism wherein the air is generated by a closure at the velar position, rather than an air-stream generated by the lungs. The back of the tongue is raised against the velum, and articulations are made farther forward by the lips or front parts of the tongue, drawing air into or pushing air out of the mouth. The clicks of some African languages are produced in this way. In English, they may be heard in the 'tut tut' sound. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/VelaricProperty]

Buccal_Property.definition: GOLD: A subclass of place properties roughly referring to positions inside the mouth. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/BuccalProperty]

Coronal_Property.definition: GOLD: Properties of sounds produced with passive articulators either lying on the coronal axis, with the blade of the tongue raised from its neutral position, or in the neutral position (for non-coronal sounds). [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/CoronalProperty]

Dorsal_Property.definition: GOLD: The class of properties associated with sounds made with the body of the tongue. Almost all vowels can be described using subclasses of this property. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/DorsalProperty]

Radical_Property.definition: GOLD: The class of place properties used to classify articulatory gestures made with the root of the tongue. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/RadicalProperty]

Labial_Property.definition: GOLD: Gestures involving the lips are said to be Labial. From the linguistic point of view the places of articulation can usefully be classified into a smaller number of groups based on the articulators they share. If consonants in which either the upper or lower lip is involved as an articulator are classified as Labials then there are three place classes among Labial sounds: the lower lip can articulate with the upper lip (bilabial), or the upper teeth (labiodentals); and, the upper lip can also be the target for the tongue (linguo-labial). [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LabialProperty]

Lateral_Property.definition: GOLD: Obstruction of the airstream at a point along the center of the oral tract, with complete closure between one or both sides of the tongue and the roof of the mouth. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LateralProperty]

Trill_Property.definition: GOLD: A term in the phonetic classification of consonant sounds on the basis of their manner of articulation: also known as trilled consonant, or a roll, 'trill' refers to any sound made by the rapid tapping of one organ of articulation against another. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/TrillProperty]

Anterior_Property.definition: GOLD: Properties characterized by focusing on the upper passive articulator on the roof of the mouth. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/AnteriorProperty]

Apicality_Property.definition: GOLD: Properties characterized by focusing on the action of the lower, active articulator, i.e. which part of the tongue is used in articulation. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/ApicalityProperty]

Backness_Property.definition: GOLD: A feature of vowel quality that correlates the difference between frequencies of formant two and formant one (overtones corresponding to a resonating frequency of the air in the vocal tract). [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/BacknessProperty]

Height_Property.definition: GOLD: The class of features describing sounds based on the relative vertical position of the tongue. Note, Ladefoged refers to this feature as High. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/HeightProperty]

Alveolar.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds produced with the alveolar ridge as the passive articulator. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Alveolar]

Dental.definition: GOLD: A consonant which involves the teeth, normally the upper teeth, as the passive articulators in its articulation. The tip or apex of the tongue usually acts as the active articulator. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Dental]

Postalveolar.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds produced with the area just behind the center of the alveolar ridge as the passive articulator. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Postalveolar]

Apical.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds produced by the tip of the tongue. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Apical]

Laminal.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds produced by the blade of the tongue. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Laminal]

Sublaminal.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds produced by the underside of the tip of the tongue. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Sublaminal]

Front.definition: GOLD: A sound made with the front part of the tongue, in the area of the hard palate. The highest point of the tongue is in the front of the mouth. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Front]

Back.definition: GOLD: A vowel sound produced with the tongue retracted towards the back of the oral cavity, e.g. [a:] as in English 'calm' or [u:] as in English 'soon'. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Back]

Central.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds produced with the tongue near the center of the mouth (along the front-back dimension). [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Central]

High.definition: GOLD: Description of the actual articulatory characteristics of vowels, and taken to specify the highest point of the tongue. In this view each vowel is characterized in terms of the distance of the highest point of the tongue from the roof of the mouth. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/High]

Mid.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds articulated between the high and low tongue positions. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Mid]

Low.definition: GOLD: Articulated with the highest point of the tongue more or less maximally distant from the roof of the mouth. In the SPE feature system, a distinctive feature defined as 'articulated with the body of the tongue below the neutral position.' [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Low]

Stop.definition: GOLD: A term used in the phonetic classification of speech sounds on the basis of their manner of articulation. It refers to any sound which is produced by a complete closure in the vocal tract. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Stop]

Fricative.definition: GOLD: Fricative sounds are those in which a turbulent airstream is produced within the vocal tract. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Fricative]

Approximant.definition: GOLD: This term is used to classify sounds based on their manner of articulation. Sounds possessing this trait are those in which the involved articulators approach one another, but not close enough to produce audible friction. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Approximant]

Trill.definition: GOLD: The vibration of one speech organ against another, driven by the aerodynamic conditions. One of the soft moveable parts of the vocal tract is placed close enough to another surface, so that when a current of air of the right strength passes through the aperture created by this configuration, a repeating pattern of closing and opening of the flow channel occurs. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Trill]

Tap.definition: GOLD: A Tap 'is a sound in which a brief contact between the articulators is made by moving the active articulator directly towards the roof of the mouth.' A tap is 'usually coronal. ... Taps are most typically made by a direct movement of the tongue tip to a contact location in the dental or alveolar region.' [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Tap]

Aspirated.definition: GOLD: A sound is described as 'aspirated' when it has a greater rate of airflow than occurs in modal voice for a period of time before or after a stricture. It often accompanies a consonant which precedes a vowel, the beginning of which is unvoiced. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Aspirated]

Unaspirated.definition: GOLD: Unaspirated refers to the configuration of glottal opening, release at the oral stricture, and vocal fold vibration in which the glottal opening gesture begins at the moment that the oral closure is made, but the maximum width of the glottal opening is reached at about the mid-point of the oral closure duration and the vocal folds return to a voicing position at about the moment of release. This typically results in a weak sounding release which lacks the burst of air characteristic of aspirated phonemes. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Unaspirated]

Voiced.definition: GOLD: A fundamental term used in the phonetic classification of speech sounds, referring to the auditory result of the vibration of the vocal cords. Sounds produced while the vocal cords are vibrating are voiced. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Voiced]

Voiceless.definition: GOLD: A fundamental term used in the phonetic classification of speech sounds, referring to the auditory result of the vibration of the vocal cords. Sounds produced while the vocal cords are not vibrating are voiceless. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Voiceless]

Modal_Voice.definition: GOLD: Regular vibrations of the vocal folds at any frequency within the speaker's normal range. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/ModalVoice]

Breathy.definition: GOLD: With regard to classifications of vocal qualities, this refers to an effect produced by allowing a large amount of air to pass through the partially open glottis. Some speakers have this as a permanent characteristic of their speech patterns. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Breathy]

Creaky.definition: GOLD: A term referring to a vocal quality in phonetic sound classification in which only one end of the vocal cords vibrates, and does so very slowly. This is a permanent feature of some speakers' voices. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Creaky]

Close.definition: GOLD: In the classification of tongue movement when articulating vowel sounds, this refers to one produced with the tongue in the highest vertical position possible within the mouth without causing audible friction. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Close]

Compressed.definition: GOLD: One of the three types of Labial that can be associated with sounds involving lip compression involving the vertical movement of one lip towards the other. Such a property is associated with a normal bilabial stop. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Compressed]

Protruded.definition: GOLD: An articulatory characteristic resulting from protrusion of the lips, often resulting in the appearance of a small labial cavity forward of the teeth and bounded at the front by the inside surfaces of the lips. Often occurring with lip rounding, the protruded quality modifies the basic articulation by extending the length of the vocal tract and altering its cross-section, resulting in lowered frequencies on all formants. Back rounded vowels are commonly more protruded than front rounded vowels. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Protruded]

Retracted.definition: GOLD: A term used in phonetics to refer to the backwards movement of an articulator, especially the back of the tongue towards the velum. Retracted sounds are heard in velarization, or the centralization of front vowels. The tongue root may also be retracted. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Retracted]

Central_Escape.definition: GOLD: A consonant articulated so that air passes out the center. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/CentralEscape]

Lateral_Escape.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds produced with a release of air through the sides of the mouth. (Note, Ladefoged refers to this as lateral.) [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LateralEscape]

Plus_Nasal.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds in which the palatopharyngeal and palatoglossus muscles lower the velum, allowing air to go out through the nose. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PlusNasal]

Minus_Nasal.definition: GOLD: Characterizing sounds in which the palatal tensor muscles and the levator palatine muscle raise the velum, preventing air from escaping through the nose. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/MinusNasal]

Plus_ATR.definition: GOLD: PlusATR (Advanced Tongue Root) characterizes sounds made with the root of the tongue drawn forward and the larynx lowered so that the part of the vocal tract in the pharynx is considerably enlarged. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PlusATR]

Minus_ATR.definition: GOLD: MinusATR (Advanced Tongue Root) characterizes sounds made in which there is no advancement of the tongue root or lowering of the larynx. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/MinusATR]

Plus_Click.definition: GOLD: PlusClick refers to having the properties of a click. Clicks are stops in which the essential component is the rarefaction of air enclosed between two articulatory closures formed in the oral cavity, so that a loud transient is produced when the more forward closure is released. This uses the velaric airstream mechanism, always ingressive, and cannot be used for sounds other than stops and affricates. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PlusClick]

Minus_Click.definition: GOLD: MinusClick refers to not having the properties of a click. Clicks are stops in which the essential component is the rarefaction of air enclosed between two articulatory closures formed in the oral cavity, so that a loud transient is produced when the more forward closure is released. This uses the velaric airstream mechanism, always ingressive, and cannot be used for sounds other than stops and affricates. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/MinusClick]

Plus_Fortis.definition: GOLD: PlusFortis refers to a sound made with relatively strong degree of muscular effort and breath force. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PlusFortis]

Minus_Fortis.definition: GOLD: MinusFortis refers to a sound made without relatively strong degree of muscular effort and breath force. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/MinusFortis]

Grapheme.definition: GOLD: A Grapheme is the smallest meaningful contrastive unit in a writing system. A grapheme is an abstraction over a set of like glyphs, the actual images on the page. That is, a particular grapheme is realized by particular glyphs. More than one glyph can realize the same grapheme. For instance, the letter A and its cursive equivalent are each realizations of the grapheme Latin Capital Letter A. Crystal defines a grapheme as the minimal contrastive unit in the writing system of a language; usually enclosed in angle brackets. The grapheme <a>, for example, is realized as several allographs A, a, a, etc., which may be seen as units in complementary distribution (e.g. upper case restricted to sentence-initial position, proper names, etc.), or in free variation (as in some styles of handwriting), just as in phonemic analysis. 'Grapheme Analysis' is the main business of graphemics (or graphology). [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Grapheme]

Glyph.definition: GOLD: A Glyph is a symbol used in a writing system to represent some kind of linguistic unit, such as a single sound, a phoneme or an entire word. Glyphs are concatenated in a writing system to form orthographic parts and orthographic words. Consider the printed word 'apple'. This word contains two instances of the 'p' glyph, which is a subclass of Glyph. Instances of a Glyph share a similar shape and can be called 'shapemes'. The class Glyph is not the same as Grapheme. A Grapheme is a contrastive unit within a particular writing system. The notion of a glyph is relevant across writing systems. For instance, consider the symbol 'р' used in a printed instance of a Russian word 'русский'. Now consider the symbol 'p' used in the printed instance of an English word 'pickle'. Both symbols are instances of the same Glyph. They share the same general shape, but do not have the same phonemic value. A shape that is the visual representation of a character. It is a graphic object stored within a font. Glyphs are objects that are recognizably related to particular characters and which are dependent on particular design. Glyphs may or may not correspond to characters in a one-to-one manner. For example, a single character may correspond to multiple glyphs that have complementary distributions based upon context (e.g. final and non-final sigma in Greek), or several characters may correspond to a single glyph known as a ligature. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Glyph]

Ligature.definition: GOLD: The merging of two or more letters (often for aesthetic reasons) from which a single, independent form is derived. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Ligature]

Character.definition: GOLD: A symbol used in writing, distinguished from others by its meaning, not its specific shape; similar to grapheme. It relates to the domain of orthographies and writing. Specific to the implementation of computers and other information systems. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Character]

Orthographic_Part.definition: GOLD: An OrthographicPart is a unit of an orthography that is not orthographically independent, that is, not necessarily able to stand alone as an orthographic word set off by whitespace. In the printed instance of the word 'conceive', 'eive' is an instance of orthographic part. Note that an orthographic part is not the same as a single glyph, although, some orthographic parts are single glyphs. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/OrthographicPart]

Orthographic_Word.definition: GOLD: An OrthographicWord is a fundamental unit of an orthography, usually set off by white space and dependent on the rules of a writing system. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/OrthographicWord]

Orthographic_Phrase.definition: GOLD: An OrthographicPhrase is a sequence of orthographic words. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/OrthographicPhrase]

Orthographic_Sentence.definition: GOLD: An OrthographicSentence is a special type of orthographic phrase, usually representing a clause. In Western writing systems, an orthographic sentence is set off by white space on the left edge and some kind of punctuation, such as a period or question mark, on the right. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/OrthographicSentence]

Paragraph.definition: GOLD: A Paragraph is a self contained unit in written language composed of a sequence of orthographic sentences. Paragraphs are set off by vertical spacing, indentation or other conventions. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Paragraph]

Diacritic.definition: GOLD: An auxiliary mark or symbol added above, below or after conventional graphic signs to give more information about the pronunciation of the sound represented in writing. Such diacritic marks include acute accent, apostrophe, caret, cedilla, diaeresis or umlaut, grave accent, macron, tilde and circumflex. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Diacritic]

Digraph.definition: GOLD: A term used in phonetics/phonology and graphics/graphology to refer to a graphic unit in which two symbols have combined to form a single element in a system. In the study of reading and spelling, digraph refers to any sequence of two letters pronounced as a single sound. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Digraph]

vowels.phoneme_count: 14 vowel phonemes in the standard inventory (analysis may vary dialectally).
vowels.note: a/á and e/é are not simple length-only pairs; their quality differs as well.

consonants.orthographic_note: Some consonant phonemes are written with digraphs or a trigraph.

prosody.stress: Primary lexical stress is normally on the first syllable.
prosody.intonation: Carries clause-type, discourse and affective information.
prosody.length: Vowel and consonant duration participate in contrast and morphophonology.

vowel_harmony.definition: Morphophonological dependency in which many suffix vowels alternate according to the backness/rounding properties of the stem.
vowel_harmony.allomorphy: Suffix selection is sensitive to stem vowel harmony; lexical exceptions and mixed-vowel stems occur.

phonological_processes.length_alternations: Stem-final vowel lengthening and other morphophonological alternations can occur before suffixes.
phonological_processes.consonant_assimilation: Voicing and place-related assimilation patterns occur in connected speech and morphology.
phonological_processes.palatalization: Morphophonological alternations can affect consonants in particular suffixal environments.

principles: long vowels are marked with acute/double-acute accents

Morphology.definition: GOLD&OntoLing: The branch of linguistics studying the internal structure of words, their forms, and the rules for combining meaningful units. Identifying patterns of systematic covariation between form and meaning. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Morphology]
Morphology.key_focus: Identifying patterns of systematic covariation between form and meaning.

Goals.elegant_description: Capture generalizations, not just list facts.
Goals.system_external_explanation: Link patterns to factors outside the system.

Word.definition: OntoLing: A complex concept with several distinct senses.

Lexeme.definition: OntoLing: An abstract dictionary word representing a core meaning.

Word-form.definition: OntoLing: A concrete occurrence of a lexeme in speech.

Word_token.definition: OntoLing: A specific occurrence in a text.

Morpheme.definition: GOLD&OntoLing: The smallest meaningful (sign) unit; a two-sided unit. Cannot be divided into smaller meaningful parts. The smallest functioning unit in the composition of words, and the minimal distinctive unit of grammar. Morphemes are commonly classified into free forms (morphemes which can occur as separate words) and bound forms (morphemes which cannot so occur - mainly affixes). A further distinction may be made between lexical and grammatical morphemes; the former are morphemes used for the construction of new words in a language; the latter are morphemes used to express grammatical relationships between a word and its context. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Morpheme]
Morpheme.key_properties: Cannot be divided into smaller meaningful parts.

types.Free: Can stand alone as a word.
types.Bound: Cannot stand alone, must attach to another morpheme.

Cumulation.definition: Expression of multiple meanings by a single marker.

deviations_from_additive_model.Idiomaticity: Meaning of whole is not derived from parts.

Allomorphy.definition: Variation in form of a morpheme.

deviations_from_additive_model.Fusion: Loss of clear boundary between morphemes.

types_by_expression.Non-linear: Signifier not a single, contiguous string.

Morph.definition: OntoLing: A concrete, linear realization of a morpheme.

Affix.definition: GOLD: An affix is a morpheme with an abstract meaning which can only be used when added to a root morpheme. These are classified in four different ways, depending on their position with reference to the root: suffix, prefix, circumfix and infix. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Affix]

Base_and_Root.Base_Stem: Part to which an affix attaches.

Root.definition: GOLD: The base form of a word which cannot be further analyzed without total loss of identity. Roots may be free or bound morphemes and can be classified as simple (i.e. compositionally unanalyzable in terms of morphemes) or complex/compound (i.e. certain combinations of simple root forms), though for the latter, the term 'stem' is often used. From a semantic point of view, the root generally carries the main component of meaning in a word. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Root]

Stem.definition: GOLD: Stem is the class of morphological units that are analyzable into a root and possibly one or more derivational units. Stems can occur alone and are the basis for adding inflectional units. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Stem]

Clitic.definition: GOLD: A prosodically dependent unit with syntactic freedom. Clitic is the class of units which members exhibit syntactic characteristics of a lexical unit, but show evidence of being morphologically bound to another lexical unit, the host, by being unstressed or subject to word-level phonological rules. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Clitic]

Proclitic.definition: GOLD: A proclitic is a clitic that precedes the lexical unit to which it is phonologically joined. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Proclitic]

Enclitic.definition: GOLD: An enclitic is a clitic that is phonologically joined at the end of a preceding lexical unit to form a single phonological unit. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Enclitic]

Compound.definition: GOLD: A term used widely in descriptive linguistic studies to refer to a linguistic unit which is composed of elements that function independently in other circumstances. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Compound]

Substance_Means.definition: OntoLing: Segmentable units part of the word-form.

Inflection.definition: OntoLing: Morphological relationship between word-forms of a single lexeme.

Derivation.definition: OntoLing: Morphological relationship between different lexemes.

Compounding.definition: OntoLing: Combination of two or more lexemes to form a new one.

Morphological_Operations.Word_Formation: Cover term for derivation and compounding.

Lexicon.definition: GOLD: In its most general sense, the term is synonymous with vocabulary. A dictionary can be seen as a set of lexical entries. The lexicon has a special status in generative grammar, where it refers to the component containing all the information about the structural properties of the lexical items in a language. In linguistics, ... we don't normally speak of the vocabulary of a particular language; instead, we speak of the lexicon, the total store of words available to a speaker. Very commonly, the lexicon is not regarded merely as a long list of words. Rather, we conceive the lexicon as a set of lexical resources, including the morphemes of the languages, plus the processes available in the language for constructing words from those resources. Apart from the lexicon of a language as a whole, psycholinguists are interested in the mental lexicon, the words and lexical resources stored in an individual brain. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Lexicon]

Lexical_Item.definition: GOLD: A unit of the vocabulary of a language such as a word, phrase or term as listed in a dictionary. It usually has a pronounceable or graphic form, fulfils a grammatical role in a sentence, and carries semantic meaning. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LexicalItem]

Lexicalized_Concept.definition: GOLD: Grammatical or semantic category expressed by a lexical item, e.g. English 'make' + 'dead' together are lexicalized as 'kill', in German 'tot' + 'machen' > 'töten', or the close linking of lexical items in an idiomatic phrase. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/LexicalizedConcept]

Inflectional_Paradigm.definition: OntoLing: The complete set of grammatical word-forms of a lexeme.
Inflectional_Paradigm.Inflection_Class: Group of lexemes sharing the same set of forms.
Inflectional_Paradigm.Syncretism: Two or more functions expressed by the same form.
Inflectional_Paradigm.Periphrasis: Use of a separate word or phrase.

Grammatical_Meaning.definition: OntoLing: Meanings obligatorily expressed by the grammar.
Grammatical_Meaning.Grammatical_Category: A set of mutually exclusive, obligatory meanings.
Grammatical_Meaning.Grammeme: An individual value within a category.

Key_Categories_for_Nouns.Agreement_Class_Gender: Classifies nouns based on agreement patterns.

Case.definition: OntoLing: Marks syntactic and/or semantic role.

Aspect.definition: OntoLing: Presents situation from internal temporal perspective.

Tense.definition: OntoLing: Locates event relative to moment of speech.

Syntax-Morphology_Interface.lexical_integrity: Syntactic rules cannot access internal morphological structure.

Productivity.definition: OntoLing: Ability to apply to new bases.
Productivity.blocking: Existing word prevents formation of synonym.

Part_Of_Speech_Property.definition: GOLD: The property that identifies the grammatical class of a word. The main 'parts of speech' recognized by most school grammars derive from the work of the ancient Greek and Roman grammarians, primarily the noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, adjective, preposition, conjunction and interjection, with article, participle, and others often added. Because of the inexplicitness with which these terms were traditionally defined and the restricted nature of their definitions, it has become preferable to use such terms as word-class or form-class, where the grouping is based on formal criteria of a more universally applicable kind. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/PartOfSpeechProperty]

Noun.definition: GOLD: A term used in the grammatical classification of words, traditionally defined as the 'name of a person, place or thing,' but the vagueness associated with the notions of 'name' and 'thing' (e.g. is 'beauty' a thing?) has led linguistic descriptions to analyze this class in terms of the formal and functional criteria of syntax and morphology. In linguistic terms, nouns are items which display certain types of inflection (e.g. of case or number), have a specific distribution (e.g. they may follow prepositions but not, say, modals), and perform a specific syntactic function (e.g. as subject or object of a sentence). Nouns are generally subclassified into common and proper types, and analyzed in terms of number, gender, case and countability. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Noun]

Proper_Noun.definition: GOLD: ProperNoun, also referred to as proper names, is the class of nouns that are used to address particular persons or culturally significant personages or places. They refer to specific entities and are not usually with articles, modifiers, possessors. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/ProperNoun]

Common_Noun.definition: GOLD: CommonNouns refer to a class of objects, places, ideas, and so on. This is in contrast with ProperNoun. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/CommonNoun]

Verb.definition: GOLD: A Verbal is a part of speech whose members typically signal events and actions; constitute, singly or in a phrase, a minimal predicate in a clause; govern the number and types of other constituents which may occur in the clause; and, in inflectional languages, may be inflected for tense, aspect, voice, modality, or agreement with other constituents in person, number, or grammatical gender. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Verbal]

Adjective.definition: GOLD: An adjectival, or 'adjective', is a part of speech whose members modify nouns. An adjectival specifies the attributes of a noun referent. Note: this is one case among many. Adjectivals are a class of modifiers. An adjectival may be inflected as comparative or superlative. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Adjectival]

Adverb.definition: GOLD: An adverbial, or 'adverb', narrowly defined, is a part of speech whose members modify verbs for such categories as time, manner, place, or direction. An adverbial, broadly defined, is a part of speech whose members modify any constituent class of words other than nouns, such as verbs, adjectives, adverbs, phrases, clauses, or sentences. Under this definition, the possible type of modification depends on the class of the constituent being modified. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Adverbial]

Adposition.definition: GOLD: An adposition is a part of speech whose members are of a closed set and occur before or after a complement composed of a noun phrase, noun, pronoun, or clause that functions as a noun phrase and forms a single structure with the complement to express its grammatical and semantic relation to another unit within a clause. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Adposition]

Preposition.definition: GOLD: A preposition is an adposition that occurs before its complement. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Preposition]

Postposition.definition: GOLD: A postposition is an adposition that occurs after its complement. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Postposition]

Pronoun.definition: GOLD: A Pronoun is a ProForm which functions like a noun and substitutes for a noun or noun phrase. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Pronominal]

Determiner.definition: GOLD: A Determiner is a part of speech whose members belong to a class of noun modifiers and express the reference, including quantity, of a noun. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Determiner]

Article.definition: GOLD: An article is a member of a small class of determiners that identify a noun's definite or indefinite reference, and new or given status. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Article]

Conjunction.definition: GOLD: A term used in the grammatical classification of words to refer to an item or a process whose primary function is to connect words or other constructions. The conventional subclassification of these 'connective' items distinguishes co-ordinating conjunctions (e.g. and, or, but) and subordinating conjunctions (e.g. because, when, unless) -- also referred to as 'co-ordinators' and 'subordinators' respectively. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Conjunction]

Interjection.definition: GOLD: An interjection is a part of speech, typically brief in form, such as one syllable or word, whose members are used most often as exclamations or parts of an exclamation. An interjection, typically expressing an emotional reaction, often with respect to an accompanying sentence, is not syntactically related to other accompanying expressions, and may include a combination of sounds not otherwise found in the language. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Interjection]

Particle.definition: GOLD: A term used to refer to an invariable item with grammatical function, especially one which does not readily fit into a standard classification of parts of speech. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Particle]

Classifier.definition: GOLD: In grammar, a morpheme whose function is to indicate the formal or semantic class to which items belong are sometimes called classifiers, e.g. -ly is an adverb classifier, -ess is a 'femininity' classifier. The marking of lexical items as belonging to the same semantic class is an important feature in many languages (e.g. Chinese, Vietnamese, Hopi), and sometimes quite unexpected bases of classification are found, in terms of shape, size, colour, movability, animacy, status and so on. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Classifier]

Numeral.definition: GOLD: A numeral is a partOfSpeech whose members function most typically as adjectives or pronouns and express a number, or relation to the number, such as one of the following: quantity, sequence, frequency, fraction. [GOLD URI: http://purl.org/linguistics/gold/Numeral]

Morphosyntactic_Property.definition: GOLD: MorphosyntacticFeature is the class of linguistic features that govern the grammatical behavior of morphosyntactic units. E.g., two morphosyntactic units can agree according to shared morphosyntactic features. Morphosyntactic features are also called grammatical categories. This class is intended to represent only the formal aspects of morphosyntax; that is, there is no notional component.
